title: III. Conversations And Exhortations Of Father Zossima
paragraphs: (e) The Russian Monk and His Possible Significance

Fathers and teachers, what is a monk? In educated circles nowadays, some pronounce the word with a sneer, others use it as an insult, and this contempt for the monk keeps growing. It's true, alas, it's true, that there are many sluggards, gluttons, profligates, and shameless beggars among monks. Educated people point to them: "You're idlers, useless to society, you live off the labor of others, you're shameless beggars." And yet how many meek and humble monks there are, yearning for solitude and fervent prayer in peace! These are noticed less, or passed over in silence. And how surprised people would be if I told them that it's from these meek monks, yearning for solitary prayer, that Russia's salvation may come once again! For they are, in truth, being made ready in peace and quiet "for the day and the hour, the month and the year." Meanwhile, in their solitude, they preserve the image of Christ, fair and undefiled, in the purity of God's truth, handed down from the days of the early Fathers, the Apostles, and the martyrs. And when the time comes, they'll hold it up before the world's faltering creeds. That's a great thought. That star will rise out of the East.

That's my view of the monk—is it wrong? Is it too proud a claim? Look at worldly people, and all those who set themselves above God's people—hasn't God's image and His truth been distorted in them? They have science; but in science there's nothing but what falls within the reach of the senses. The spiritual world, the higher part of man's being, is rejected outright, dismissed almost triumphantly, even with hatred. The world has proclaimed the reign of freedom, especially lately, but what do we actually see in this freedom of theirs? Nothing but slavery and self-destruction! Because the world says:

"You have desires, so satisfy them, for you have the same rights as the richest and most powerful. Don't be afraid to satisfy them—multiply them, even." That's the modern doctrine of the world. That's what they call freedom. And what comes of this right to multiply one's desires? In the rich, isolation and spiritual suicide; in the poor, envy and murder; because they've been granted rights, but never shown the means to satisfy their wants. They claim the world is growing more and more united, more and more bound together in brotherly community, as it conquers distance and sends thoughts flying through the air.

Alas, put no faith in such a bond. Treating freedom as the multiplication and quick satisfaction of desires, people distort their own nature, since it breeds in them countless senseless, foolish desires, habits, and absurd fancies. They live only for mutual envy, for luxury and display. Having dinners, visits, carriages, rank, and slaves to wait on you is treated as a necessity, one for which life, honor, and human feeling get sacrificed, and people even kill themselves if they can't satisfy it. We see the same thing among those who aren't rich, while the poor drown their unsatisfied wants and their envy in drink. But soon they'll be drinking blood instead of wine—they're being led toward it. I ask you, is such a man free? I once knew a "champion of freedom" who told me himself that when he was denied tobacco in prison, he was so miserable at the deprivation that he nearly betrayed his own cause just to get tobacco again! And a man like that says, "I'm fighting for the cause of humanity."

How can a man like that fight? What is he fit for? He might manage some quick, isolated act, but he can't hold out for long. And it's no wonder that, instead of gaining freedom, they've sunk into slavery, and instead of serving the cause of brotherly love and human unity, they've fallen instead into discord and isolation, just as my mysterious visitor and teacher told me in my youth. And that's why the idea of serving humanity, of brotherly love and the solidarity of mankind, is dying out more and more in the world, and this idea is even treated with mockery at times. Because how can a man shake off his habits? What's to become of him if he's so enslaved to the habit of satisfying the countless desires he's created for himself? He's isolated, and what does the rest of humanity matter to him? They've succeeded in piling up a greater mass of possessions, but there's less joy in the world.

The monastic way is entirely different. Obedience, fasting, and prayer are laughed at, and yet only through them does the path to real, true freedom lie. I cut off my superfluous, unnecessary desires, I subdue my proud, willful nature and discipline it through obedience, and with God's help I attain freedom of spirit, and with it, spiritual joy. Which is more capable of conceiving a great idea and serving it—the rich man in his isolation, or the man who's freed himself from the tyranny of material things and habits? The monk is reproached for his solitude: "You've shut yourself away within monastery walls for your own salvation, and forgotten the brotherly service of humanity!" But we'll see who turns out to be more devoted to the cause of brotherly love. Because it isn't we who are isolated, but they, even though they don't see it. In the old days, leaders of the people came from among us, so why shouldn't they again? The same meek and humble ascetics will rise up and go out to labor for the great cause. Russia's salvation comes from the people. And the Russian monk has always stood with the people. We're isolated only if the people are isolated. The people believe as we do, and an unbelieving reformer will never accomplish anything in Russia, even if he's sincere at heart and a genius. Remember that! The people will meet the atheist and overcome him, and Russia will be one and orthodox. Take care of the peasant and guard his heart. Keep educating him, quietly. That's your duty as monks, for the peasant carries God in his heart.
(f) On Masters and Servants, and Whether They Can Be Brothers in Spirit

Of course I don't deny that there's sin in the peasants too. And the fire of corruption is spreading visibly, hour by hour, working its way down from above. The spirit of isolation is descending on the people too. Moneylenders and devourers of the village commune are on the rise. Already the merchant grows more and more hungry for rank, strives to appear cultured though he hasn't a trace of it, and toward that end meanly looks down on his own old traditions, even feels ashamed of his fathers' faith. He calls on princes, though he's nothing but a corrupted peasant himself. The peasants are rotting away in drunkenness and can't shake the habit. And what cruelty toward their wives, even toward their children! All from drink! I've seen children of nine in the factories, frail, rickety, stooped, already corrupted. The stifling workshop, the din of machinery, work all day long, foul language, and drink, drink—is that what a small child's heart needs? He needs sunlight, childish play, good examples all around him, and at least a little love. There must be no more of this, monks—no more tormenting children—rise up and preach against it, hurry, hurry!

But God will save Russia, for though the peasants are corrupted and can't renounce their filthy sin, they still know it's accursed by God and that they do wrong in sinning. So our people still believe in righteousness, still have faith in God, and still weep tears of devotion.

It's different with the upper classes. Following science, they want to base justice on reason alone, no longer on Christ as before, and they've already declared that there's no such thing as crime, no such thing as sin. And that's only consistent, because if there's no God, what does crime even mean? In Europe the people are already rising up violently against the rich, and their leaders are everywhere driving them toward bloodshed, teaching them that their rage is righteous. But their "rage is cursed, for it is cruel." But God will save Russia, as He's saved her many times before. Salvation will come from the people, from their faith and their meekness.

Fathers and teachers, watch over the people's faith and this won't remain a dream. All my life I've been struck by the dignity of our great people, their true and fitting dignity. I've seen it myself, I can testify to it, I've seen it and marveled at it, I've seen it despite the degrading sins and poverty-stricken appearance of our peasantry. They aren't servile, and even after two centuries of serfdom they're free in manner and bearing, yet without insolence, without vengefulness, without envy. "You're rich and well-born, you're clever and gifted—fine, be so, God bless you. I respect you, but I know that I too am a man. By respecting you without envy, I prove my own dignity as a man."

In truth, if they don't say this in so many words—since they don't yet know how to put it into words—that's how they act. I've seen it myself, known it myself, and, would you believe it, the poorer our Russian peasant is, the more noticeable that serene goodness becomes, since the richer among them are for the most part already corrupted, and much of that is due to our own carelessness and indifference. But God will save His people, for Russia is great in her humility. I dream of seeing, and seem already to see clearly, our future. It will come to pass that even the most corrupt of our rich will end up feeling ashamed of his riches before the poor, and the poor, seeing his humility, will understand and yield before him, will respond joyfully and kindly to his honorable shame. Believe me, it will end that way; things are already moving toward it. Equality is to be found only in the spiritual dignity of man, and only among us will that be understood. If we were truly brothers, fraternity would exist, but before that, people will never agree on how to divide up wealth. We preserve the image of Christ, and it will shine out like a precious diamond to the whole world. So may it be, so may it be!

Fathers and teachers, a touching thing happened to me once. On my travels I met, in the town of K., my old orderly, Afanasy. It had been eight years since I'd parted from him. He happened to spot me in the marketplace, recognized me, ran up to me—and how delighted he was! He simply pounced on me: "Dear master, is that you? Is it really you I'm seeing?" He took me home with him.

He was no longer in the army; he was married and already had two small children. He and his wife earned their living selling goods in the marketplace. His room was poor, but bright and clean. He made me sit down, put on the samovar, sent for his wife, as though my arrival were a holiday for them. He brought his children to me: "Bless them, Father."

"Is it for me to bless them? I'm only a humble monk. I'll pray for them. And for you, Afanasy Pavlovitch, I've prayed every day since that day, because it all began with you," I said. And I explained that to him as best I could. And what do you think? The man kept staring at me, unable to believe that I, his former master, an officer, now stood before him in this guise and this position; it brought him to tears.
"Why are you crying?" I said, "you should rejoice over me instead, dear friend, whom I can never forget, for my path is a glad and joyful one."
He didn't say much, but kept sighing and shaking his head over me tenderly.
"What became of your fortune?" he asked.
"I gave it to the monastery," I answered; "we live in common there."

After tea I began saying my good-byes, and suddenly he brought out half a rouble as an offering to the monastery, and I saw him hurriedly pressing another half-rouble into my hand as well: "That's for you, for your travels, it may come in useful, Father."

I took his half-rouble, bowed to him and his wife, and went out rejoicing. And on my way I thought: "Here we both are now, he at home and I on the road, sighing and shaking our heads, no doubt, and yet smiling joyfully in the gladness of our hearts, remembering how God brought about our meeting."

I never saw him again after that. I had been his master and he my servant, but now, exchanging a loving kiss with softened hearts, there was a great human bond between us. I've thought a great deal about that, and here's what I think now: is it really so unimaginable that this grand, simple-hearted unity might one day become universal among the Russian people? I believe it will come to pass, and that the time is near.

And about servants I'll add this: in the old days, when I was young, I was often angry with servants—"the cook served something too hot, the orderly didn't brush my clothes properly." But what taught me better then was a thought of my dear brother's, which I'd heard from him in childhood: "Am I worth it, that another person should serve me and be ordered about by me, in his poverty and ignorance?" And I marveled at the time that such simple, self-evident ideas should be so slow to occur to us.

It's impossible for there to be no servants at all in the world, but act so that your servant may be freer in spirit than if he weren't a servant at all. And why couldn't I be a servant to my own servant, and even let him see it, without any pride on my part or mistrust on his? Why shouldn't my servant be like my own family, so that I could take him into my household and rejoice in doing it? Even now this can be done, but it will lead, in the future, to the grand unity of mankind, when a man will no longer seek out servants for himself, or desire to turn his fellow creatures into servants as he does now, but instead will long with his whole heart to be the servant of all, just as the Gospel teaches.

And can it really be a dream that in the end man will find his joy only in deeds of light and mercy, rather than in the cruel pleasures of today—gluttony, lechery, vanity, boasting, and envious rivalry with one another? I firmly believe it isn't, and that the time is near. People laugh and ask, "When will that time come, and does it even look like coming?" I believe that with Christ's help we'll accomplish this great thing. And how many ideas has human history seen that were unthinkable ten years before they came to be! Yet when their appointed hour arrived, they emerged and spread across the whole earth. So it will be with us too, and our people will shine forth before the world, and all men will say: "The stone which the builders rejected has become the cornerstone of the building."

And we may well ask the scoffers themselves: if our hope is only a dream, when will you build your own edifice and order the world justly through reason alone, without Christ? If they claim they're the ones advancing toward unity, only the most simple-minded among them actually believe it, so much so that one can only marvel at such naïveté. In truth, they have far more far-fetched dreams than we do. They aim at justice, but, denying Christ, they'll end up flooding the earth with blood, for blood cries out for blood, and he who takes up the sword will perish by the sword. And if it weren't for Christ's covenant, they'd slaughter one another down to the last two men left on earth. And even those last two men wouldn't be able to restrain their pride toward each other, and one would kill the other, and then himself. And that is exactly what would happen, were it not for Christ's promise that for the sake of the humble and meek, those days shall be cut short.

While I was still wearing my officer's uniform, after my duel, I talked about servants in polite society, and I remember everyone was amazed at me. "What!" they'd ask, "are we supposed to have our servants sit down on the sofa and offer them tea?" And I answered: "Why not, at least now and then?" Everyone laughed. Their question was frivolous and my answer wasn't very clear, but there was some truth in the thought behind it.
(g) On Prayer, Love, and Contact with Other Worlds

Young man, never forget to pray. Every time you pray, if your prayer is sincere, there will be some new feeling in it, some new meaning, and this will give you fresh courage; you'll come to understand that prayer is itself an education. And remember too, every day, whenever you're able, to repeat to yourself, "Lord, have mercy on all who stand before You today." For every hour, every moment, thousands of people leave this life on earth, and their souls stand before God. And how many of them depart alone, unknown, sad, dejected, with no one to mourn for them or even know whether they lived at all! And behold, from the other end of the earth, perhaps, your prayer for their rest may rise up to God, though you never knew them, nor they you. How moving it must be, for a soul standing in fear before the Lord, to feel in that very instant that someone, somewhere, is praying for him too, that there's still a fellow creature left on earth who loves him! And God will look upon you both more graciously, for if you've had that much pity on him, how much more pity will He have, He who is infinitely more loving and merciful than you! And He will forgive him for your sake.

Brothers, have no fear of men's sin. Love a man even in his sin, for that reflects Divine Love and is the highest form of love on this earth. Love all of God's creation, the whole of it and every grain of sand in it. Love every leaf, every ray of God's light. Love the animals, love the plants, love everything. If you love everything, you'll perceive the divine mystery within things. Once you perceive it, you'll begin to understand it more fully every day. And in the end you'll come to love the whole world with an all-embracing love. Love the animals: God has given them the beginnings of thought and untroubled joy. Don't disturb that, don't torment them, don't deprive them of their happiness, don't work against God's purpose. Man, don't take pride in your superiority to the animals; they are without sin, while you, for all your greatness, defile the earth by your very presence on it, and leave the traces of your corruption behind you—alas, that's true of nearly every one of us! Love children especially, for they too are sinless, like angels; they live to soften and purify our hearts, and, in a sense, to guide us. Woe to anyone who wrongs a child! Father Anfim taught me to love children. That kind, quiet man used to spend, on our travels, the few coins we were given on sweets and cakes for children. He could never pass a child without being moved. That's simply the man's nature.

At certain thoughts one stands baffled, especially at the sight of men's sin, wondering whether to meet it with force or with humble love. Always resolve to use humble love. If you settle on that once and for all, you can subdue the whole world. Loving humility is a marvelously strong thing, the strongest thing there is, and there is nothing else like it.

Every day, every hour, every minute, examine yourself, watch yourself, and make sure your bearing is a fitting one. You pass by a small child—you pass by spiteful, with ugly words, with an angry heart; you may not have even noticed the child, but he's seen you, and your image, unfitting and ignoble, may lodge itself in his defenseless heart. You don't know it, but you may have planted a seed of evil in him, and it may grow, all because you weren't careful in front of the child, because you hadn't cultivated in yourself a careful, actively benevolent love. Brothers, love is a teacher, but one has to know how to acquire it, for it's hard to acquire, it comes at a high price, it's won slowly through long labor. Because we have to love not just occasionally, for a moment, but forever. Anyone can love occasionally—even the wicked can do that.

My brother once asked the birds to forgive him; that sounds senseless, but it's right, because everything is like an ocean, everything flows and blends together; a touch in one place sets off a ripple at the other end of the earth. It may be senseless to beg forgiveness from the birds, but the birds would be happier beside you—a little happier, at least—and so would children, and every animal, if you were nobler than you are now. It's all like an ocean, I tell you. Then you'd pray to the birds too, consumed by an all-embracing love, in a kind of rapture, and pray that they too would forgive you your sin. Treasure that ecstasy, however senseless it may look to others.

My friends, pray to God for gladness. Be glad as children are, as the birds of heaven are. And don't let men's sin throw you off in what you're doing. Don't be afraid that it will wear away your work or keep it from being accomplished. Don't say, "Sin is powerful, wickedness is powerful, our surroundings are corrupting, and we're alone and helpless, and our environment is wearing us down and stopping our good work from being done." Flee from that despair, children! There's only one path to salvation—so take it: make yourself responsible for all men's sins. That's the truth, friends, believe me, for the moment you sincerely make yourself responsible for everything and everyone, you'll see at once that it really is so, that you're to blame for every person and everything. But if you throw your own idleness and weakness onto others, you'll end up sharing Satan's pride, and murmuring against God.

As for the pride of Satan, here's what I think: it's hard for us on earth to grasp it fully, and so it's easy to fall into error and share in it, even imagining we're doing something grand and fine. In fact, many of the strongest feelings and impulses of our nature we simply cannot grasp while on earth. Don't let that be a stumbling block, and don't imagine it can serve as an excuse for anything. For the Eternal Judge asks of you what you're capable of understanding, not what you're not. You'll know that for yourself hereafter, for then you'll see all things truly and won't dispute them. Here on earth, in truth, we walk as if lost, and if it weren't for the precious image of Christ before us, we'd be undone and utterly lost, just as the human race was before the flood. Much on earth is hidden from us, but to make up for it, we've been given a precious, mystical sense of our living bond with the other world, the higher heavenly world, and the roots of our thoughts and feelings lie not here but in other worlds. That's why philosophers say we cannot grasp the true reality of things on earth.

God took seeds from different worlds and sowed them on this earth, and His garden grew up, and everything that could sprout came up, but what grows lives, and stays alive, only through its sense of contact with those other, mysterious worlds. If that feeling weakens or is destroyed in you, the heavenly growth within you will wither away. Then you'll grow indifferent to life, even come to hate it. That's what I believe.
(h) Can a Man Judge His Fellow Creatures? Faith to the End

Remember above all that you cannot be anyone's judge. For no one can judge a criminal until he recognizes that he himself is just as much a criminal as the man standing before him, and that he, perhaps, bears more blame than anyone for that very crime. Once he understands that, he'll be fit to be a judge. Absurd as that may sound, it's true. If I myself had been righteous, perhaps there would have been no criminal standing before me at all. If you can take upon yourself the crime of the person your heart is judging, do it at once—suffer for him yourself, and let him go without a word of reproach. And even if the law itself makes you his judge, act in that same spirit as far as you're able, for he will go away and condemn himself far more bitterly than you ever could. If, after your kiss, he walks away untouched, mocking you, don't let that trip you up. It only means his time hasn't come yet, but it will come in due course. And if it never comes, no matter; if not him, then someone else in his place will come to understand, and suffer, and judge and condemn himself, and the truth will still be fulfilled. Believe that, believe it without a shadow of doubt, for in that belief lies the whole hope and faith of the saints.

Work without ceasing. If, as you're falling asleep at night, you remember, "I haven't done what I ought to have done," get up at once and do it. If the people around you are spiteful and indifferent and won't listen to you, fall down before them and beg their forgiveness, for in truth you are to blame for their unwillingness to listen. And if you can't reach them in their bitterness, serve them in silence and humility, without ever losing hope. If everyone abandons you, even drives you away by force, then, once you're left alone, fall to the earth and kiss it, soak it with your tears, and it will bear fruit even though no one has seen or heard you in your solitude. Believe to the very end, even if every other person has gone astray and you're the only one left faithful; bring your offering even then, and praise God in your loneliness. And if two of you are gathered together, then that is a whole world, a world of living love. Embrace each other tenderly and praise God, for even if His truth has been fulfilled only in the two of you, that is enough.

If you yourself sin, and grieve even unto death over your sins, or over some sudden lapse, then rejoice for others instead—rejoice for the righteous man, rejoice that if you have sinned, he is righteous and has not sinned.

If men's wrongdoing stirs you to indignation and overwhelming distress, even to a desire for vengeance against the wrongdoers, shun that feeling above all else. Go at once and seek out suffering for yourself, as though you yourself were guilty of that wrong. Accept that suffering, bear it, and your heart will find comfort, and you'll come to understand that you too are guilty, since you might have been a light to the wrongdoers, as the one sinless man was, and you were not a light to them. If you had been a light, you'd have lit the way for others too, and the wrongdoer might perhaps have been saved from his sin by your light. And even if your light was shining, and yet you see that others weren't saved by it, stand firm, and don't doubt the power of that heavenly light. Believe that if they weren't saved then, they'll be saved later. And if they're not saved later, their sons will be saved, for your light won't die out even after you're dead. The righteous man passes away, but his light remains. People are always saved after the deliverer's death. People reject their prophets and kill them, but they come to love their martyrs and honor those they've slain. You're working for the whole, you're acting for the future. Don't seek a reward, for your reward on this earth is already great: the spiritual joy granted only to the righteous man. Don't fear the great or the powerful, but be wise and forever serene. Know the measure of things, know the seasons—study that. When you're left alone, pray. Love to throw yourself down on the earth and kiss it. Kiss the earth and love it with an unceasing, consuming love. Love all men, love everything. Seek out that rapture, that ecstasy. Water the earth with the tears of your joy, and love those tears. Don't be ashamed of that rapture, treasure it, for it's a gift from God, and a great one; it isn't given to many, only to the chosen.
(i) On Hell and Hellfire: A Mystical Reflection

Fathers and teachers, I ponder this: "What is hell?" I hold that it's the suffering of being unable to love. Once, in an infinite existence beyond measure in time and space, a spiritual being was granted, on coming into this world, the power to say, "I am, and I love." Once, only once, he was given a moment of active, living love, and for that purpose earthly life was granted him, along with its seasons and its times. And that fortunate being rejected the priceless gift, failed to prize it or love it, scorned it, and remained indifferent. Such a man, having left the earth, sees Abraham's bosom and speaks with Abraham, as we're told in the parable of the rich man and Lazarus, and beholds heaven, and can even go up to the Lord. But that is precisely his torment—to rise up to the Lord having never loved, to be brought close to those who did love, after having despised their love. For he sees it clearly and says to himself, "Now I understand, and though I now thirst to love, there'll be nothing great in my love, no sacrifice in it, because my earthly life is over, and Abraham won't come, not even with a single drop of living water"—that being the gift of active earthly life—"to cool the burning thirst of spiritual love now blazing in me, the very love I scorned while on earth; there's no more life left for me, and there will be no more time! Even if I'd gladly give my life for others now, it can never happen, because that life, the one that could have been sacrificed for love, is over, and now a gulf lies fixed between that life and this existence."

They speak of hellfire in the literal, material sense. I won't go into that mystery, and I steer clear of it. But I think that if there really were fire in the material sense, they'd almost be glad of it, since I imagine that in physical agony their still greater spiritual agony would be forgotten, if only for a moment. What's more, that spiritual agony cannot be taken from them, because that suffering isn't external, it lies within them. And if it could somehow be taken away, I think it would only be bitterer still for those unhappy souls. For even if the righteous in Paradise forgave them, watching their torment, and called them up to heaven out of infinite love, that would only multiply their torment, since it would awaken in them, even more sharply, a burning thirst for a responsive, active, grateful love that is now impossible for them. In the timidity of my heart, though, I imagine that the very recognition of this impossibility might in the end serve to console them. For by accepting the love of the righteous alongside the impossibility of ever repaying it, through this submission and the working of this humility, they'll come at last to something like a semblance of that active love they once scorned in life, something resembling its outward form.... I'm sorry, friends and brothers, that I can't put this more clearly. But woe to those who've taken their own lives on earth, woe to suicides! I believe there can be no one more wretched than they are. We're told it's a sin to pray for them, and outwardly the Church, as it were, renounces them, but in the secrecy of my own heart I believe we may pray for them too. Love can never be an offense to Christ. For souls such as these I've prayed silently my whole life, I confess it, fathers and teachers, and even now I pray for them every day.

Oh, there are some who remain proud and fierce even in hell, despite their certain knowledge and contemplation of the absolute truth; there are terrible ones who've given themselves over entirely to Satan and his proud spirit. For these, hell is voluntary and endlessly consuming; they are tormented by their own choice. For they have cursed themselves, cursing God and life itself. They feed on their own vindictive pride like a starving man in the desert sucking blood from his own body. But they're never satisfied, and they refuse forgiveness, curse the God who calls to them. They cannot look upon the living God without hatred, and they cry out that the God of life should be annihilated, that God should destroy Himself and His own creation along with Him. And they will burn forever in the fire of their own wrath, yearning for death and annihilation. But they will never attain death....

Here Alexey Fyodorovitch Karamazov's manuscript ends. Let me repeat, it's incomplete and fragmentary. The biographical details, for instance, cover only Father Zossima's earliest youth. As for his teachings and opinions, we find sayings gathered together that were clearly spoken on very different occasions. His remarks during the last few hours haven't been kept separate from the rest, but their general character can still be gathered from what we have in Alexey Fyodorovitch's manuscript.

The elder's death came, in the end, quite unexpectedly. Although those gathered around him that last evening realized his death was approaching, it was still hard to imagine it would come so suddenly. On the contrary, his friends, as I mentioned already, seeing him that night so apparently cheerful and talkative, were convinced there'd been at least a temporary turn for the better in his condition. Even five minutes before his death, they said afterward, marveling, it was impossible to foresee it. He seemed to suddenly feel a sharp pain in his chest, went pale, and pressed his hands to his heart. Everyone rose from their seats and hurried to him. But even in his suffering, he still looked at them with a smile, sank slowly from his chair to his knees, then bowed his face to the ground, stretched out his arms, and, as though in joyful rapture, praying and kissing the ground, quietly and joyfully gave up his soul to God.

News of his death spread at once through the hermitage and reached the monastery. The deceased's closest friends, along with those whose position required it, began preparing the body according to the ancient ritual, and all the monks gathered together in the church. And before dawn, news of the death had reached the town. By morning the whole town was talking of the event, and crowds were streaming out from town to the monastery. But that subject will be dealt with in the next book; here I'll only add that before a day had passed, something happened so unexpected, so strange, so upsetting and bewildering in its effect on the monks and the townspeople, that even after all these years, that day of general suspense is still vividly remembered in the town.
PART III
